header: Date: 2025-12-03 | Time: 14:30 PST | Duration: 48m\nAttendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood Solutions), Lina Ortiz (Pegasus - Platform), Marcus Hale (Pegasus - SRE), Devon Park (Pegasus - CTO), Sara Nguyen (Pegasus - Security)
summary: Discovery focused on how Redwood handles zone isolation and graceful degradation across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments. Main asks: expected RTO/RPO for regional failures, fallback policy options (route, model degrade, queueing), SLA guarantees, and what Pegasus needs for an internal benchmark. Customer emphasized compliance (SOC2, KMS, audit logs). Agreed next steps: share architecture note, run a benchmark, draft runbook/canary plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we wanted to walk through how Redwood thinks about zone isolation and graceful degradation across our modes, quick intros?
[00:22] Devon Park: yeah hi Devon here, CTO at Pegasus, we'll be focused on availability constraints, we run real-time assistants in the app so latency spikes are visible.
[00:36] Lina Ortiz: Lina, platform engineer, i handle infra and failover runbooks, also curious about what we need to change in our traffic router.
[00:46] Marcus Hale: Marcus, SRE, will ask the tough questions like, when a whole AZ goes down what actually happens to in-flight requests.
[00:58] Arjun Patel: thanks, ok so at a high-level Redwood has three levers: routing fallback (re-route to healthy region), model variants (degrade to quantized/smaller model), and operational throttles (queueing or shedding). We can combine them per-route.
[01:20] Lina Ortiz: when you say "re-route" is that automatic? or do we need to run a control-plane change?
[01:28] Arjun Patel: good question, for Hosted we do automated health checks and smart routing by policy, so you can set failover policy to auto fail to "region-b" or to fall back to a compatible model variant in the same region. For Dedicated/Private you can choose automated or manual policies depending on isolation needs.
[01:52] Marcus Hale: okay but SLA-wise, what do you commit to for a region outage? like RTO targets?
[02:02] Maya Chen: our public SLA for Hosted focused on uptime is 99.9% baseline today, but for Dedicated we offer higher uptime contracts and a playbook for multi-region attachments; typical RTO we design for is in the 1-5 minute window for routing cutover, depends on DNS TTLs and client retry logic.
[02:30] Devon Park: 1-5 minutes is a big range, our product metrics are sensitive at 30s p95. Can you actually deliver seamless in 30s for P95?
[02:42] Arjun Patel: the reality is there are layers: client-side retry, edge proxys, and in-flight token generation. For very low p95 windows we recommend a hybrid approach: keep a lightweight small-model warm in the secondary region (prefix/KV cache priming) so on cutover you route to that variant and preserve sub-250ms p95 for most traffic. It's not magic, it's pre-warmed state.
[03:12] Lina Ortiz: pre-warmed KV cache - is that something you manage or we have to maintain?
[03:20] Arjun Patel: Redwood manages cache priming for Hosted and can for Dedicated if you allow cross-region replication; for Private deployments we provide the tooling and playbook but Pegasus would host the replication job (we can automate it as part of onboarding).
[03:36] Marcus Hale: and what about data residency - if we replicate KV to another region do we run afoul of residency or compliance?
[03:44] Jules Park: short answer: you control where replicas live. For customers with residency constraints we recommend a same-country standby region or degrade to a model variant in-region rather than cross-border replication.
[03:58] Devon Park: what's the failback path, once the primary recovers do you auto-shift back or is it manual?
[04:08] Arjun Patel: configurable - many teams prefer a canary-based failback: once primary passes health checks for a sustained window we do canary routing for a percentage then full shift. We can also use time-based automatic fallback if you want.
[04:26] Lina Ortiz: how are partial degradations handled - like some features ok to be slower, others not?
[04:34] Maya Chen: we support per-route policies, so you can say route A (real-time chat) must prioritize latency and fallback to smaller model; route B (batch summarization) can be queued or routed to async batch tier.
[04:48] Marcus Hale: curious about quantization—if we switch to quantized weights to save latency/cost, does that change output quality significantly?
[04:56] Arjun Patel: there's a tradeoff; for many prompts quality delta is small but we always recommend eval sets. Redwood Optimize can run a quick AB test and provide recommended quantization profile per route - helps find sweet spot between 5-20% latency improvement and minimal quality delta.
[05:16] Devon Park: and operationally, when an AZ failover happens, do we lose in-flight responses? do they retry?
[05:24] Arjun Patel: depends on where the session lives. If KV cache is lost mid-stream there may be partial degradation; we try to preserve session by streaming partial results and instructing client to retry last chunk. We also support checkpointing across tokens in some model formats to resume, but it's model and runtime dependent.
[05:46] Lina Ortiz: Ping — you mentioned 'checkpoint' how mature is that? we've seen models drop context.
[05:52] Arjun Patel: checkpointing is emerging; we support token-level checkpoint on a best-effort for some runner combos. For strict guarantees we recommend session persistence in the app and idempotent replays.
[06:08] Marcus Hale: switching gears - what observability do we get so our SREs can monitor and trigger mitigation?
[06:14] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route latency dashboards, token-level cost, tracing hooks. You can wire up alerts on p95/p99, error rates, and also export audit logs for every request.
[06:30] Sara Nguyen: audit logs - do they include payloads or just metadata? we need to avoid exfiltration of PII.
[06:36] Jules Park: logs are metadata by default; payload capture is opt-in and can be routed to your private storage with redaction rules. For Private deployments you keep everything in your VPC.
[06:52] Lina Ortiz: what about key management for encryption at rest — HSM or KMS?
[06:57] Maya Chen: we integrate with major KMS providers and support customer-managed keys on Dedicated/Private and Bring-Your-Own-HSM patterns for on-prem.
[07:07] Marcus Hale: great. Ok, let's talk about concrete SLOs you typically see — your public numbers vs what customers actually observe in practice?
[07:16] Arjun Patel: publicly we talk about SLO targets e.g., p95 300-500ms for short sequences on large instances, but in practice it varies heavily with prompt length. Most customers target p95 1-2s for conversational mixing; Dedicated customers tuning instance class can get sub-400ms p95 for short chats.
[07:40] Devon Park: that's useful. I want to know how graceful degradation looks under heavy load — do you throttle, queue, or fail early?
[07:48] Arjun Patel: Redwood has an overload policy engine. Options: 1) shed cheap requests (low priority), 2) throttle token generation (slower but accept), 3) fall back to cached responses for highly repetitive prompts, 4) switch to small-model variant. You configure priorities per route.
[08:08] Lina Ortiz: can fallbacks be chained? like try small-model then region fallback?
[08:14] Arjun Patel: yes, we support chained fallbacks with order and observable knobs so the routing decision tree is auditable.
[08:24] Marcus Hale: during our initial pilot we want to validate two scenarios: AZ fail + region intact and full region failure. What would you recommend for tests?
[08:34] Arjun Patel: for AZ fail keep region fallback disabled and simulate instance termination to validate local failover; for region fail test cold start recovery and model warmup - run sustained ramp to ensure caches warm and measure p95/p99 during cutover. We'll provide a test harness script.
[08:58] Maya Chen: note: DNS and client retry behavior is often the biggest invisible factor. Recommend low TTLs and exponential backoff.
[09:06] Devon Park: any example runbook steps you can share now?
[09:10] Arjun Patel: quick outline: 1) detect via health probes -> 2) mark zone unhealthy -> 3) shift traffic to standby variant/region -> 4) prime KV cache if possible -> 5) monitor canary -> 6) promote back after sustained green. We'll send a fleshed-out doc.
[09:30] Lina Ortiz: licensing/contract question — if we run Dedicated with reserved capacity across regions is that an extra cost?
[09:38] Maya Chen: yes reserved capacity is per-pool; multi-region standby will have cost implications (warm standby capacity) but we can design burst policies to reduce always-on costs. We'll show cost tradeoffs in the table Arjun is going to prepare.
[09:56] Marcus Hale: security question: can we require that fallbacks never cross certain regions?
[10:02] Jules Park: absolutely — policies can be region-restricted. You can define allowed failover targets per route or account.
[10:10] Sara Nguyen: what's the typical time to onboard Private with two-region setup?
[10:16] Maya Chen: depends on environment; for VPC-based Private with us managing control plane it's often 4-6 weeks; fully on-prem air-gapped tends to be 8-12 weeks.
[10:28] Devon Park: timeline matters for us — if we go Dedicated + multi-region standby how quickly can you get us a pilot?
[10:34] Maya Chen: we can start a small pilot in 2-3 weeks once legal and infra access are done. SE will run the pilot and benchmarks.
[10:42] Lina Ortiz: one more - alerts. will Redwood send alerts to our pager?
[10:48] Arjun Patel: yes you can hook into PagerDuty, Slack, Opsgenie. Alerts are configurable by threshold and route.
[10:56] Marcus Hale: any gotchas with on-prem network egress? we have strict egress rules.
[11:02] Jules Park: for on-prem we support air-gapped packages and a private control plane; small agent for metrics and tracing can be configured to offline-forward. We'll include a network matrix.
[11:18] Devon Park: ok let's recap and next steps.
[11:22] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood will send architecture note for zone/region failover, Arjun will produce a latency/cost degrade table, we'll provide test harness, and Pegasus will run a benchmark next Tue. Any other outstanding blockers?
[11:36] Lina Ortiz: please include the recommended config for canary thresholds in the runbook.
[11:42] Maya Chen: will do.
[11:44] Devon Park: thanks all.
[11:46] [crosstalk] Marcus Hale: thanks, appreciate it.
[11:50] Maya Chen: end.
notes: Transcript has minor transcription errors (KV cash sometimes transcribed), casual talk, and occasional speaker label swaps. The session included explicit security and compliance questions and concluded with clear next steps and action items.
